definitions.definition: (also loaf of bread) A block of bread after baking.

quote.citation: 1913, Joseph C[rosby] Lincoln, chapter VIII, in Mr. Pratt’s Patients, New York, N.Y., London: D[aniel] Appleton and Company, →OCLC:
quote.text: Philander went into the next room […] and came back with a salt mackerel that dripped brine like a rainstorm. Then he put the coffee pot on the stove and rummaged out a loaf of dry bread and some hardtack.

definitions.definition: Any solid block of food, such as meat or sugar.

quote.citation: 1627 (indicated as 1626), Francis [Bacon], “IV. Century.”, in Sylua Syluarum: Or A Naturall Historie. In Ten Centuries. […], London:  […]  William Rawley […]; [p]rinted by J[ohn] H[aviland] for William Lee […], →OCLC:

definitions.definition: (Cockney rhyming slang) Ellipsis of loaf of bread: the brain or the head.[1]

quote.citation: 1960, P[elham] G[renville] Wodehouse, “VIII AND XII”, in Jeeves in the Offing, London: Herbert Jenkins, →OCLC:
quote.text: It is frequently said of Bertram Wooster that he is a man who can think on his feet, and if the necessity arises he can also use his loaf when on all fours. [...] “Why didn't the idiot tell her not to open it?” “It was his first move. ‘I've found a letter from you here, precious,’ she said. ‘On no account open it, angel,’ he said. So of course she opened it.” She pursed the lips, nodded the loaf, and ate a moody piece of crumpet. “So that's why he's been going about looking like a dead fish.”

definitions.definition: A solid block of soap, from which standard bar soap is cut.
(cellular automata) A particular still life configuration with seven living cells.

quote.citation: 1989 November 20, Dean Hickerson, “Life: glider gun origin”, in comp.theory.cell-automata‎[1] (Usenet):
quote.text: It runs for 17331 generations before stabilizing as 136 blinkers, 109 blocks, 65 beehives, 18 loaves, 18 boats, 7 ships, 4 tubs, 3 ponds, 2 toads, and 40 gliders.

quote.citation: 1992 September 10, David Bell, “Spaceships in Conway's Life (Part 3b)”, in comp.theory.cell-automata‎[2] (Usenet):
quote.text: Running a LWSS into it can produce various debris. One of these reactions produces a loaf. When the loaf is properly hit with other LWSSs, it can be pulled backwards.

quote.citation: 1998 January 27, Ian Osgood, “Life: looking for smallest ancestor of a quad-loaf”, in comp.theory.cell-automata‎[3] (Usenet):
quote.text: I am looking for the smallest ancestor of the following four loaf pattern in Conway's Game of Life:

definitions.definition: (Can we verify(+) this sense?) (Internet slang) To assume or be in catloaf position (for cats or other animals)

etymologies.etymologyHTML: Probably a back-formation from loafer.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To do nothing, to be idle.

quote.citation: 2015, Elizabeth Royte, Vultures Are Revolting. Here’s Why We Need to Save Them., National Geographic (December 2015)[4]
quote.text: They don’t (often) kill other animals, they probably form monogamous pairs, and we know they share parental care of chicks, and loaf and bathe in large, congenial groups.
